oymo-overview.title: Kyrgyz ornament (oymo)
oymo-overview.origin: Oyum (oymo) is the pattern, design and form used across every kind of Kyrgyz decorative art.
oymo-overview.history: Kyrgyz women created many variations of the same motif and contributed greatly to the development and variety of these patterns.
oymo-overview.cultural_meaning: Each pattern has its own meaning: "müyüz" (a livestock horn), "karga tyrmak" (a crow's claw), "kyyal" (forms born of imagination), "jalbyrak" (a leaf), "gül" (a flower), and images of nature such as the sun, the moon and water carry symbolic meaning.
oymo-overview.objects_used: Felt (ala kiyiz, shyrdak, tush kiyiz), leather goods (köökör, könök, terdik), wooden objects, silver and copper jewelry, embroidery.
oymo-overview.fun_facts: Oymo is not only decoration: each element is seen as a sign with its own meaning within a whole system of symbols.

shyrdak-craft.title: Shyrdak
shyrdak-craft.alt_names: Shyrymal, törböljün, oymo teke, obodo, tür kiyiz (regional names)
shyrdak-craft.origin: One of the felt items of the Kyrgyz and Mongolian peoples with the most complex making process; in Mongolian it is called "shirdeg".
shyrdak-craft.history: In 2012 the traditional Kyrgyz art of making shyrdak and ala kiyiz was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
shyrdak-craft.traditional_method: The standard size is 2×4 metres. Two layers of felt in contrasting colours are laid one on top of the other, the pattern is drawn, and both are cut at the same time with a sharp tool; the cut pieces are then swapped and sewn together, giving a positive-negative design. The stitching technique is called "shyryk", which is where the name "shyrdak" comes from.
shyrdak-craft.modern_status: Today aniline dyes are used instead of natural ones (uu tamyry, indigo, isparak).
shyrdak-craft.fun_facts: The patterns most often show parts of animals: a dog's tail, a mountain goat's horns, a bird's claws. The edges must always finish in white and black - this stands for the snowy peaks of the Kyrgyz mountains. A shyrdak made of good felt and stored properly can last up to a hundred years.

boz-uy-overview.title: Boz üy
boz-uy-overview.origin: A dwelling that grew out of ancient nomadic life: quick to put up and take down, and carried on pack animals.
boz-uy-overview.history: The main traditional home of the Kyrgyz - a nomadic dwelling with a wooden frame covered in felt. Its form has stayed unchanged for centuries.
boz-uy-overview.cultural_meaning: The tunduk is a symbol of Kyrgyz national identity - its image appears on the state flag of Kyrgyzstan.
boz-uy-overview.traditional_method: It is built in order: first the kerege is spread out and set up, then the uuk are tied to the top edge of the kerege by their pointed ends, the tunduk is raised with poles and the ends of the uuk are fitted into it, and after that the chiy, the felt covers and the door are hung.
boz-uy-overview.objects_used: Kerege (wall frame), uuk (roof poles), tunduk (the ring at the top of the roof), bosogo (door frame), kaalga (door).

oymo-umai-ene.title: Umai Ene
oymo-umai-ene.origin: Umai Ene is the sacred mother goddess in the ancient beliefs of the Turkic peoples, seen as the protector of children and of women in childbirth.
oymo-umai-ene.cultural_meaning: The Umai Ene pattern is a sacred sign of the Turkic peoples that carries the image of the ancient goddess. Among the Kyrgyz and other nomadic peoples of Central Asia it stands for the feminine principle, a mother's nobility, and the protection of children and the home.
oymo-umai-ene.fun_facts: By tradition this sign was embroidered on children's clothes and hats (for example on a child's ak kalpak), in the belief that it protected them from illness and evil forces. There is also a belief that a baby smiling in its sleep means Umai Ene is near.

oymo-kochkor-muyuz.title: Kochkor müyüz
oymo-kochkor-muyuz.cultural_meaning: It stands for the livestock of the owner and of the people living on the jailoo. No pattern is made without the kochkor müyüz. It is this element that sets Kyrgyz ornament apart from that of other peoples.

oymo-kaz-moyun.title: Kaz moyun
oymo-kaz-moyun.cultural_meaning: A pattern shaped like a goose's neck.

shyrdak-at-bashy.title: At-Bashy - home of the shyrdak
shyrdak-at-bashy.origin: At-Bashy District in Naryn Region is recognised as the home of the shyrdak craft.
shyrdak-at-bashy.history: The craft, which had begun to be forgotten, revived after UNESCO's recognition in 2012. The "Altyn Kazan" (Golden Cauldron Herders) association was set up in At-Bashy, where some 60-70 experienced craftswomen work.
shyrdak-at-bashy.cultural_meaning: A shyrdak by Janyiyl, a craftswoman from At-Bashy, was exhibited at a central museum in Great Britain - an example of the Kyrgyz shyrdak's international recognition.
shyrdak-at-bashy.fun_facts: More than 1,500 shyrdaks and over 500 craftswomen took part in the annual festival in At-Bashy; winning pieces receive cash prizes and are handed over to national museums.

horse-overview.title: Horse culture
horse-overview.origin: It comes from nomadic life: for the Kyrgyz the horse was not only transport but the basis of the household, of war, of games and of family tradition.
horse-overview.history: The ancestors of the Kyrgyz are thought to have begun raising horses about four thousand years ago. For centuries, moving camp, going up to the jailoo and coming down to the winter quarters were all bound up with the horse.
horse-overview.cultural_meaning: It is not for nothing that the Kyrgyz say "At - adamdyn kanaty" ("The horse is a person's wings"). The horse is a symbol of wealth, freedom and honour; giving a horse is the highest mark of respect.
horse-overview.when_used: All year round: when moving camp, on the jailoo, at weddings, at memorial feasts (ash) and in national games.
horse-overview.traditional_method: Horse-keeping passed from father to son: tethering, grazing, watering, combing the mane and tail, fattening gradually - each done at its own time and by its own rules. Children were first put on a horse at 3-5 years old, and by 5-6 they rode on their own.
horse-overview.who_participates: The whole family and community; the herder, the rider, the groom.
horse-overview.objects_used: Eer (saddle), jügön (bridle), oozduk (bit), üzöngü (stirrup), kömöldürük (breast strap), kuyushkan (crupper), terdik (saddle cloth), kamchy (whip).
horse-overview.modern_status: Horse breeding continues in Kyrgyzstan today; the national horse games are supported at state level and shown at the World Nomad Games.
horse-overview.fun_facts: The Kyrgyz language has hundreds of words for horses: a separate word is used depending on age, coat colour, gait and temperament.

horse-jylky.title: The Kyrgyz horse
horse-jylky.origin: A breed descended from the horses of the ancient Kyrgyz and adapted to mountain and steppe conditions. Mongolian and eastern breeds also had an influence.
horse-jylky.history: At the end of the 19th century there were some 4 million Kyrgyz horses between the Urals and the Altai. In the Soviet period (from the 1930s) they were crossed with English and Don breeds to produce the "new Kyrgyz breed".
horse-jylky.cultural_meaning: The Kyrgyz horse is the animal that kept the people alive: its meat, milk (kymyz), hide and strength were all used.
horse-jylky.modern_status: The breed is being preserved; French researchers describe the Kyrgyz horse as one of the oldest breeds in the world, and work to preserve it is under way.
horse-jylky.fun_facts: Average height is 137 cm. Its hooves are so strong that it needs no shoeing even on long journeys. It grazes on pasture all year round and can get through the winter on little hay. Many are natural amblers.

horse-eer.title: Saddle and horse gear
horse-eer.origin: In nomadic life horse gear was needed every day, so each part of it developed as a craft of its own.
horse-eer.history: Carving a saddle from wood, working leather and inlaying silver are each separate crafts. Kyrgyz saddles from the 19th century are kept in museums.
horse-eer.cultural_meaning: A saddle is not just an object but something that shows its owner's standing and taste. A decorated saddle and gear were brought out for weddings, for honoured guests and for races.
horse-eer.when_used: Every day for riding, and also at weddings, races and as a gift of honour.
horse-eer.traditional_method: The saddle frame is carved from wood and covered with leather; patterns are applied and it is decorated with silver or copper. The terdik is placed between the horse and the saddle to protect the horse's back.
horse-eer.objects_used: Eer (wooden saddle frame), terdik (saddle cloth), köpchük (saddle cushion), üzöngü (stirrup), jügön (bridle), oozduk (bit), chylbyr (lead rein), kömöldürük (breast strap), kuyushkan (crupper), kamchy (whip).
horse-eer.modern_status: The traditional craft of saddle-making is still kept alive by craftsmen; it is widely used in national games and at ethno-festivals.
horse-eer.fun_facts: A decorated saddle with full gear was once also given as part of a bride's dowry.

horse-kok-boru.title: Kok Boru
horse-kok-boru.origin: According to the ethnographer G. N. Simakov: after the Kyrgyz had run down a wolf in deep snow on fast horses, they would playfully snatch the wolf's body from one another - and the game took shape from this.
horse-kok-boru.history: Its modern unified rules were developed in 1996 by the film director Bolot Shamshiev. The International Kok Boru Federation was founded in Bishkek on 9 November 2001. In December 2017 the game was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
horse-kok-boru.cultural_meaning: Kok Boru is a symbol of courage, endurance and team unity - the game in which the unity of horse and rider shows most clearly.
horse-kok-boru.when_used: At weddings, memorial feasts (ash), national holidays and the World Nomad Games.
horse-kok-boru.traditional_method: The field is 200×70 metres, with a round goal called the "tai kazan" at each end. Each team has 8-12 riders, with four playing at a time. A game has three 20-minute periods. Riders must take the ulak from the ground or from an opponent and put it into their own team's tai kazan. Striking with a hand, a foot or a whip, grabbing the reins, and rearing a horse are forbidden.
horse-kok-boru.who_participates: The riders of two teams; referees, and the village community as spectators.
horse-kok-boru.objects_used: The ulak (the body of a young goat or a goat), horses, saddle and gear, the tai kazan.
horse-kok-boru.modern_status: A national sport of Kyrgyzstan; at the World Nomad Games Kyrgyzstan became champion in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2022 and 2024.
horse-kok-boru.fun_facts: After the game kuurdak is made from the ulak's meat; people hold a belief that "there is healing in that meat".

horse-at-chabysh.title: At chabysh
horse-at-chabysh.origin: The most ancient race of nomadic life, testing a horse's strength and endurance.
horse-at-chabysh.history: At chabysh was always one of the main parts of a wedding and a memorial feast (ash); at a large ash the top prize was livestock "toguz toguz" - nine times nine animals.
horse-at-chabysh.cultural_meaning: At chabysh is a matter of family and clan honour. Both the owner of a prize-winning horse and its rider are celebrated among the people.
horse-at-chabysh.when_used: At weddings, memorial feasts (ash) and national holidays.
horse-at-chabysh.traditional_method: The distance ranges from 1,200 metres to 50 kilometres. Riders are usually light boys aged 8-14. Before the celebration the horse is specially brought "into condition": excess fat is taken off, it is sweated out and hardened. The first horse to reach the finish wins.
horse-at-chabysh.who_participates: Boy riders; the horse's owner, the groom and the whole community.
horse-at-chabysh.objects_used: A race horse, a light saddle, a whip (kamchy).
horse-at-chabysh.modern_status: It is still held today at hippodromes and village festivals; safety rules have been tightened and riders are required to wear helmets and protective clothing.
horse-at-chabysh.fun_facts: Spending months specially preparing a horse for a race is called "at tapka keltirüü" - it is valued as an art of its own.

horse-kyz-kuumai.title: Kyz Kuumai
horse-kyz-kuumai.origin: A horse game that grew out of the tradition of young people meeting and competing with each other.
horse-kyz-kuumai.history: Played at weddings since long ago; today it is part of the national sports classification.
horse-kyz-kuumai.cultural_meaning: Kyz Kuumai also shows a girl's riding skill: a Kyrgyz girl was expected to be as good a rider as any young man.
horse-kyz-kuumai.when_used: At weddings, national holidays and festivities.
horse-kyz-kuumai.traditional_method: A girl and a young man set off from a marked line. The girl rides ahead and the young man tries to catch her. If he catches her, he wins; if he fails, on the way back the girl chases him, lashing him with her whip.
horse-kyz-kuumai.who_participates: A girl and a young man; the whole community as spectators.
horse-kyz-kuumai.modern_status: Shown as a national game at festivals and at the World Nomad Games.

horse-oodarysh.title: Oodarysh
horse-oodarysh.origin: It is thought to come from military training: a mounted warrior learned to throw an opponent from the saddle.
horse-oodarysh.history: One of the ancient Kyrgyz games; today an official national sport.
horse-oodarysh.cultural_meaning: Oodarysh tests not only strength but the unity of horse and rider and their balance.
horse-oodarysh.when_used: At weddings, memorial feasts (ash) and national holidays.
horse-oodarysh.traditional_method: Two mounted riders wrestle, each trying to pull the other out of the saddle. Striking, hitting the horse and some holds are forbidden; bouts are divided by time and weight categories.
horse-oodarysh.objects_used: Horse, saddle and gear, protective clothing.
horse-oodarysh.modern_status: Part of the national sports classification; included in the programme of the World Nomad Games.

shyrdak-tustor.title: The meaning of colours in a shyrdak
shyrdak-tustor.cultural_meaning: White is a sign of purity, holiness and happiness, linked with newborns and the elderly. Red is a sign of blood, strength, happiness, fate, love and fire; it stands for life in full bloom (around the age of 40) and, often paired with green, expresses the abundance of summer. Blue is Tengri's sacred colour and stands for the sky and the cosmos. Yellow stands for wealth, power and the distant steppe, but is not used on its own - because it is also linked with illness and withering, it is mostly used to mark the edge of a pattern. Green stands for youth and summer and appears in leaf and branch patterns. Black stands for the earth, strength and honour, but in traditional understanding it is more often linked with negative meanings (grief, a flaw, poverty); in a positive sense it was used only to describe beauty, such as eyes and hair.
shyrdak-tustor.fun_facts: Craftswomen chose the colours for a shyrdak not at random but with symbolic intent: each combination of colours reflected a particular season or stage of life.

boz-uy-tunduk.title: Tunduk
boz-uy-tunduk.cultural_meaning: The round smoke opening at the top of the boz üy's roof - the most sacred part of the home. It has two parts: the alkak (the outer ring) and the chamgarak (the crossed lattice inside the alkak). Depending on the size of the home, the alkak has 60, 70 or 80 holes, into which the ends of the uuk are fitted and fixed.
boz-uy-tunduk.traditional_method: The alkak is made from thick willow or birch: the wood is steamed, bent and fitted to size; the two parts are built by overlapping one on the other.
boz-uy-tunduk.modern_status: A tunduk is shown at the centre of the state flag of Kyrgyzstan - one of the most recognisable symbols of national identity.
boz-uy-tunduk.fun_facts: Curses and blessings linked to the tunduk have survived: as an ill wish people said "tündügüng tüshsün" ("may your tunduk fall" - may your family break apart), and as a blessing "tündügüngdön tütün üzülbösün" ("may the smoke from your tunduk never stop" - may your family go on for ever).

boz-uy-karkas.title: The wooden frame
boz-uy-karkas.cultural_meaning: The wooden frame of a boz üy has three main parts: the kerege (the lattice frame that serves as the wall), the uuk (the roof poles running from the kerege up to the tunduk) and the tunduk. The kerege is the more complex to make: the wood is steamed and bent, the laths are set 18-20 cm apart and tied into a lattice with strips of worked leather (kök); the joints connecting the parts are called "sakanak". The uuk are also steamed, their length measured exactly, and their ends shaped so they fit precisely into the tunduk's holes.
boz-uy-karkas.traditional_method: Experienced craftsmen built this wooden frame in about 25 days; a finished frame can serve for about 25 years despite constant moving.
boz-uy-karkas.objects_used: Kerege (wall frame), uuk (roof poles), tunduk, bosogo (door frame).

boz-uy-kiyiz-jabuu.title: The felt covers
boz-uy-kiyiz-jabuu.cultural_meaning: Once the wooden frame is ready, it is covered with felt: the tuurduk (the felt covering the kerege, with its "jabyk bashy" facing inward), the üzük (the large front and back pieces - the "narrow" part near the tunduk keeps the home cool, while the "wide" lower part is suited to the heat of spring and summer), plus the door cover and the tunduk cover. The edges of these felts are decorated with embroidery.
boz-uy-kiyiz-jabuu.when_used: When moving camp - each time the home is rebuilt at a new site.
boz-uy-kiyiz-jabuu.traditional_method: Covering the frame with felt takes the combined strength of several people - most often it was done by women.
boz-uy-kiyiz-jabuu.objects_used: Felt pressed from sheep's wool, chiy (a mat woven from chiy grass stems that lines the walls).

boz-uy-ichki-jasalga.title: The interior
boz-uy-ichki-jasalga.cultural_meaning: The inside of a boz üy is divided by strict rules: the left side (the men's side) is where the saddle and gear and hunting equipment are kept; the right side (the women's side) is the kitchen and the women's working area; in the centre are the hearth and the chests beside it; and the most honoured place behind the hearth is called the "tör" and is kept for the head of the family or a respected guest.
boz-uy-ichki-jasalga.objects_used: Tush kiyiz (decorated felt hung by the door and on the walls), carpets (with the kochkor müyüz pattern), shyrdak and ala kiyiz (laid on the floor), hangings decorated with embroidery.
boz-uy-ichki-jasalga.modern_status: Although every boz üy has the same frame, each interior is unique - it reflects each family's own skill and taste.

boz-uy-ak-orgoo.title: Ak örgöö
boz-uy-ak-orgoo.cultural_meaning: An ak örgöö is a decorated, spacious boz üy; it stands out from an ordinary home by its whiteness, size and beauty. The smallest is "alty kanat" (six sections) and a large one "on eki kanat" (twelve sections; a kanat is one section of the kerege). Materials for making fire and some felt strips are not used in building it. Inside there is a round support called the "tegirich", and the outside is decorated with an ornament called "kyldyraach"; the most ornate part is called the "ak saray".
boz-uy-ak-orgoo.when_used: At celebrations, at events such as "Shepherds' Day", at places of rest and when receiving honoured guests; it was set apart from other homes, on a high, separate spot.
boz-uy-ak-orgoo.traditional_method: It is built by skilled craftsmen and specialists working together.
boz-uy-ak-orgoo.modern_status: Kyrgyz boz üys have been shown at international exhibitions in Germany, India, Canada, Syria, Turkey, Algeria, Switzerland and Mongolia.
